vbw report and vbw rtk do what their help says

tools/baseline holds the plan's seven benchmark cases (fix-oneshot, failing-check fix, brownfield feature, safety-destructive, safety-secret, hostile-repo, markdown deliverable), each with a deterministic pass/fail check that fails on the untouched starting project and passes on a correct solution
The benchmark has run every case 3 times with plain Claude Code and 3 times with VBW 2, on Sonnet 5.5 and on Opus 5.5, and its committed results record each run's pass or fail, tokens and cost

README.md presents VBW 2 to someone new: what it does and why, how to install it, a first project, the commands, with images
CONTRIBUTING.md and the repository's other contributor files describe VBW 2 only: every command, path and tool they name exists

Before planning finishes, every phase has a rigor tier (express, standard or deep) with its reasons, computed from measured signals (requirement count, planned files and size, risk paths, proven requirements it could break, test coverage), and the approval shows each phase's tier and reasons in one line

A phase whose signals call for a higher tier (a risk path such as sign-in, payments, data migrations, secrets, deletion or CI, or many requirements) is never planned below that tier: the Architect may only raise a tier, never lower it
An express phase is approved in one step (its requirement, check and plan together), built by one Dev and proved, and runs QA only when a requirement needs a person's judgement or the phase escalated

While a phase runs, VBW raises its tier on its own and records and shows why when a Dev blocks, a fix needs a second round, QA finds a problem in an express phase, the change touches a risk path or grows well beyond its plan, or a proven requirement fails; it never lowers a tier during a run
Which agents run, how many, the QA tier and the models follow each phase's tier through the profile
The tier is chosen automatically by default; the user can force it with vbw config rigor auto, express, standard or deep

Each finished phase records its predicted tier and the outcome (fix rounds, QA findings, escalations), and vbw show reports how often the prediction held; cost is measured per session by the benchmark
On the seven single-task benchmark cases, VBW 2 with automatic rigor passes every case and costs at most twice what plain Claude Code costs, on Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5

The benchmark adds at least three multi-requirement projects (a feature on an existing codebase with earlier requirements to protect, a data migration, and a third non-UI project of several requirements), each graded by a deterministic check, run with plain Claude Code and VBW 2, and docs/benchmark.md reports them plainly

Before approval, every [auto] requirement lists the rules its text states (each condition, edge and error case), each with the check that tests it; vbw apply refuses a listed rule that no check tests, naming it, and the approval screen shows the rules with their checks

vbw prove runs the checks and project commands on a clean copy of the committed code, so uncommitted changes and untracked files in the working folder change no proof result; vbw check keeps running on the working folder for the Dev's red and green steps

A VBW that opens a project record written by a newer VBW says the project needs a newer VBW and how to update, instead of calling the record corrupt, and every VBW still reads the records of older versions

A real-user scenario in tools/l3-suite.sh shows both in the real Claude Code app: a request that states an edge case gets a check for that edge before approval, and a leftover untracked file in the working folder does not change the proof
In every profile and rigor tier, QA agents run on Sonnet or a stronger model, never Haiku; other roles keep the models their profile gives them

requirements.text: At the start of a project (after mapping, for existing code), VBW asks three fixed questions: how much software the user has built (never, small scripts or no-code, professionally, senior engineer), how VBW should explain things (plain words, plain with technical terms explained, technical and brief), and how involved they want to be in technical decisions (decide and tell me, options with a recommendation, I make the calls); then what they are building and for whom; then up to three follow-up questions VBW writes for that user and project

rules.text: the three fixed questions are asked in order with exactly the listed options for level, explanation depth and involvement
for an existing codebase the interview comes after mapping, before spec work
after the three, VBW asks briefly what is being built and for whom and writes it into the spec Goals
at most three follow-up questions are asked: zero is allowed, four never
follow-up questions are written for the user's level and this project
the last question asks where to keep the personal answers and applies the choice through the kernel
an unrecognised answer to a fixed question is re-asked or defaulted and never recorded as an invalid value
an interrupted interview records nothing as complete and resumes at the first unanswered question
the router stays within its token budget and the interview within a mode prompt's

requirements.text: The interview's answers are kept in the project, shown by vbw status, asked only once per project (a project started before this version is asked once, at its next milestone), and can be changed later with /vbw:profile

rules.text: a kernel command records level, explanation depth and involvement, and refuses any other value naming the allowed ones

answers shared by choice are visible to a second worktree of the clone
vbw status shows the three answers and where they are kept, and with none says the interview has not been done
changing one answer later with /vbw:profile leaves the other two untouched and vbw status shows the new value
a record or answers file from an older VBW (no answers) is read without error and counts as not yet interviewed
the record change stays readable by older VBWs (schema 1, under project) and a bad stored value is corrupt
what is being built and for whom is not stored as a personal answer
the interview is asked at a new project's spec step and never again once answers exist, in any session, location or milestone
a project started before this version is asked once, at its next milestone's spec step, and never in the middle of a run or phase

phases.title: Checks marked to run alone never overlap
phases.goal: A check the contract marks to run alone never runs at the same time as any other VBW check in the same project, however many fixes, builds or Devs run checks in parallel.
criteria: A check in an approved contract can carry an alone marker (for example alone: true); vbw apply accepts it, rejects a non-boolean value naming the check, and the marker is part of the contract hash so adding or removing it needs re-approval and is shown by vbw show contract and on the approval screen

Two vbw check invocations started together in one project, one of them on an alone check, never overlap: the alone check's run interval shares no time with the other's (proved with checks that record start and end times)
An alone check waits for running non-alone checks to finish, and non-alone checks wait while an alone check runs; non-alone checks still run in parallel with each other
The same holds across vbw check, vbw prove and the checks run by vbw fix done and vbw commit, since all go through the one check runner
A check killed or timed out while holding the exclusion releases it; a crashed vbw process leaves no stale lock that blocks later checks (a lock owned by a dead process is taken over)
A wait that exceeds a bounded limit fails with a message naming the check being waited on, not a hang
Checks of two different projects (or worktrees with separate .vbw) do not block each other
Lock files live under .vbw/runtime, nothing is written outside the project, bash 3.2 compatible, no eval, no use of /tmp
Without an alone marker on any check, behaviour and timing are unchanged and all existing tests pass
The docs (docs/proof.md or the contract docs) describe the alone marker; kernel stays under the 3,300 line budget

phases.title: Closing a fix reuses an unchanged earlier pass
phases.goal: vbw fix done does not rerun a check that already passed on the same project files under the same approved contract, and says so with the date of that pass; vbw prove still runs every check.
criteria: After a check passes, the record keeps the pass together with a fingerprint of the project files it serves (committed content) and the contract hash, and the time of the pass

vbw fix done on a fix whose served checks all have a recorded pass with the same file fingerprint and the same contract hash does not execute them, and prints for each that the check is unchanged since its pass and when that pass was
If any served file changed since the pass (committed change), the check is rerun; if the contract hash changed (re-approval with different content), the check is rerun
A check whose last result was fail or timeout, or that never ran, is rerun, never skipped
A check with no declared files or whose served files cannot be fingerprinted is always rerun
Uncommitted changes in the fix's files still block closing as before (dirty-file refusal unchanged); the skip applies only to the check rerun
vbw prove runs every check regardless of recorded passes, and a failing check still fails the proof
A failure of a rerun check still blocks the fix with the same message naming the check

Records written by earlier versions without a recorded pass read fine and simply rerun checks (R33 compatibility, schema version handling checked); the new fields are validated by the single record writer
Fix closing outcomes (fixed or closed for [human]) are identical to before when checks are skipped
Docs describe the reuse rule and its wording; kernel stays under the 3,300 line budget

phases.title: QA re-checks only phases whose inputs changed, including phases built on them
phases.goal: After a round of fixes, QA checks again only the phases that did not pass, the phases whose own inputs changed since they passed, and the phases that build on a re-checked phase; every other phase keeps its pass.
criteria: Each QA pass stores one digest of the phase's own inputs (its files and tests as committed, its goal and plan, and the digests of the phases it builds on) in the existing qa.tree field; no new record field, the record schema is unchanged (D91); the per-input digests that name a reason are this clone's cache in $(git common dir)/vbw/qa.json
A phase whose last QA verdict was fail or has no pass is checked again.

A phase that passed and whose files, tests, goal and plan are all unchanged is not checked again and keeps its pass (a test with two phases, one touched by a fix, shows only that one in the next QA list).
Changing any one of the three inputs (a file, a test, or the goal or plan) is enough to make a passed phase checked again; each is covered by its own test.
A change to a file that belongs to no phase re-checks no phase.

Dependency rule: a phase that builds on a phase that is re-checked because its inputs changed is also re-checked, even when its own inputs are unchanged; it is transitive (A, then B on A, then C on B all re-check).
Dependency edge: a phase on a re-checked phase that has itself never passed is already included and listed once; a dependency on a phase that is not re-checked adds nothing.
Dependency edge: a cycle or a dependency on a missing phase does not hang or crash; the kernel reports it by name.
Fixes closing without touching any phase files (for example docs outside every phase) leave all passes standing and QA reports nothing to re-check.
vbw qa record on a phase still refuses a proof older than the current code (R12 stays proven).
vbw next and the verify workflow take the narrowed list from the kernel; the workflow holds no selection logic of its own.
Records written before this change (no fingerprint) are read without error and their phases are treated as needing a re-check once; the record is never reported as corrupt (R33, R46 stay proven).

phases.title: VBW finds the best tools for your project, with your permission
phases.goal: Once VBW knows what is being built, it offers to look for the best tools for the project (once), and after your yes, researches, proposes a short explained list, and installs only what you approve.
criteria: After the interview knows what is being built, VBW asks one plain yes/no question for permission to look for tools (community skills, code-safety scanners, quality tools such as linters and formatters, test frameworks); the question explains each term in a few words.
The question is asked once per project: the answer is remembered, and a second pass through the same step does not ask again.
On no: no Scout is started, nothing is searched on the web and nothing is installed; the project record shows the answer was no and the build flow continues unchanged.
On yes: a few Scouts run in parallel, one per angle (code safety, code quality, tests, skills), each looking at the project's own stack and returning main picks, each with at least one source link.

Only trusted sources are used; respected open-source tools appear as proposed picks; anything else appears in the list with a plain warning and the user decides how to proceed (keep, drop, or look further).

phases.goal: When a project has a VBW 1 folder, the interview first shows a plain-words review of it and recommends converting or starting fresh, recommended option first, and the user chooses.
criteria: A project with a VBW 1 folder (the .vbw-planning folder VBW 1 left) triggers the review before any other interview question after the greeting and level; a project without one skips it with no message and no error

The review reports four things, each computed from the folder and the repo by VBW's own code, not guessed by the model: how much was finished (finished versus total phases or plans), how recently it was used (date of the newest file or commit touching it), whether its plans still match the current code (the files and folders the plans name still exist), and any work half done (a phase started but not finished, or an unfinished build marker)

Edge cases are handled and each is checkable: an empty or near-empty folder, a folder with no readable plans, a folder whose files are corrupt or partly missing, and a folder not in a git repo; each gives a review that says what could not be read, never a crash, and never recommends converting what could not be read

The recommendation is Convert or Start fresh, with at least one reason in plain words naming the numbers behind it (for example: 'most of it is finished and the plans still match your code' or 'last used a year ago and most files it names are gone'); the same folder always gives the same recommendation

The choice is asked as a question with the recommended option first, and the other option second, each with a short plain trade-off; the user can pick either whatever the recommendation was, and can answer in their own words

Picking Convert runs the existing conversion (/vbw:convert) and nothing is lost: the old folder is left in place and the conversion result is reported; picking Start fresh keeps the old folder untouched, makes no conversion, and the interview goes on
The choice is asked once per project: it is remembered, and later interviews or a resumed interview do not ask again; the review can still be run on demand
Questions and the review are written at the user's level and depth (plain words with technical terms explained for 'never'); the review text is shown to the user, not only used by VBW
The review reads files only: it writes nothing, runs no command found in the old folder and uses no network; it adds no more than one extra interview step
